input: — and this is why the float continues to be held at 17%. The critical path of the upgrade project runs through the tie-ins, and a tie-in cannot get under way until the plant window has opened, which means that any slip upstream is inherited by the tie-in in full. A lower allowance, by contrast, would treat every activity as though it were going to take its planned duration, and planned durations are the durations that assume no weather stoppages, no late deliveries and no permit delays, so a programme built on that basis has no room left when any one of those things happens. The float should not be seen as spare time held against poor estimating. The float covers the delay that one completed activity passes on to the next activity in the chain, because a predecessor that finishes late, within its own allowance, hands that lateness on, and the float at the end of the chain is the only part of the programme that can absorb the accumulation. It is for this reason that the steering group holds the float at project level, since the release of float is a decision taken against the state of the whole programme rather than a concession granted activity by activity, and a lower figure agreed now would be re-argued at the first slip, on worse information. The figures behind the allowance can be found in the cost table in the Costs section and are not repeated here. What this section is asking the reader to accept is the level itself: 17% is the allowance at which the programme still finishes inside the committed window even when the ordinary delays occur, whereas the lower alternative only finishes inside the window if none of them do.
